Name: stale_evidence_anchoring_icl
Title: When the Rule Changes Mid-Prompt: Stale-Evidence Anchoring in In-Context Learning and a Cheap Cure
Short Hypothesis: Because ICL behaves like an (approximately) exchangeable Bayesian learner over latent tasks, LLMs cannot discount obsolete demonstrations: when the labeling rule changes in the middle of a context, the cost of adapting scales with the *number* of pre-switch examples rather than their recency, and the model's internal task representation becomes a count-weighted blend of old and new tasks. If this diagnosis is right, then injecting a purely inference-time recency prior into a small set of task-encoding attention heads should restore adaptivity without harming stationary ICL.
Related Work: Almost all ICL analysis assumes a *single stationary* latent task per prompt: Bayesian views and Bayesian scaling laws (Xie et al. 2022; Arora et al. 2024), task recognition vs. task learning (Pan et al. 2023; Lin & Lee 2024), context-scaling analyses (2025), concept encoding-decoding and task/function vectors (Todd et al. 2024; Hendel et al. 2023; From Context to Concept, 2025), and order/permutation sensitivity work (Lu et al. 2022; Rethinking Invariance in ICL, 2025) which explicitly treats demonstrations as exchangeable and even engineers permutation invariance. Robustness work studies *noisy or shifted candidate pools* (ConDS, 2025) and spurious features in ICL, but the noise is i.i.d. across the context, not a structured mid-context change of the ground-truth rule. Flipped-label studies (Wei et al. 2023) flip labels for the *whole* prompt. In-context RL (Algorithm Distillation, DPT, in-context model-based planning) handles non-stationary environments but measures return, not the evidence-integration rule, and offers no mechanistic account for pretrained LLMs. Our contribution is distinct on three axes: (i) we introduce mid-context task drift as a diagnostic regime that directly separates exchangeable-Bayes from recency-weighted accounts of ICL — a distinction invisible in stationary prompts; (ii) we predict and test a quantitative 'switch-cost law' relating adaptation to pre-switch example count; (iii) we derive a training-free intervention (head-selective attention discounting triggered by a drift probe) from the diagnosis, turning permutation invariance from a desideratum into an identified failure mode.
Abstract: In-context learning is almost universally studied with prompts drawn from a single stationary task, and the field has even sought permutation-invariant ICL algorithms. Yet real contexts drift: instructions get revised mid-conversation, user preferences change, tool APIs update, and streaming data shifts. We ask a simple question: what does an LLM do when the labeling rule changes in the middle of its context? We construct a controlled benchmark of drifting prompts (label remappings, in-context linear regression with a changing weight vector, boolean-function switches, output-format and language switches, and preference reversals) in which the first n_pre demonstrations follow rule A and the next n_post follow rule B, and we compare model predictions against two reference learners: an exchangeable Bayesian posterior over rules (which cannot discount stale evidence) and a recency-discounted learner. We find and characterize 'stale-evidence anchoring': post-switch accuracy is governed by the *ratio* n_post/(n_pre+n_post) rather than by absolute recency, so more pre-switch evidence makes adaptation proportionally slower — a distinct scaling law from stationary ICL curves. Mechanistically, we show via task-vector probes and logit lens that the model's internal task representation after a switch is a count-weighted convex blend of the two task encodings, and that a small set of task-encoding heads carries this blend. Finally, we show that a training-free intervention — exponential attention-logit discounting over demonstration blocks in those heads, gated by a linear 'drift detector' probe read off the residual stream — recovers most of the oracle post-switch accuracy while leaving stationary ICL intact. Small-transformer pretraining experiments reveal a stability-plasticity tradeoff: meta-training with drifting contexts yields recency-adaptive ICL at a measurable cost in stationary sample efficiency.
Experiments:
1) Benchmark construction. Six drift families: (a) label remapping (SST-2/AGNews/TREC with verbalizer set A then B, including full flips and permutations); (b) in-context linear regression (y=w_A^T x then y=w_B^T x, controllable angle between w_A,w_B) evaluated on numeric-token LLMs and small trained transformers; (c) boolean/rule induction (e.g., parity over different index subsets); (d) output-format switch (JSON -> XML, uppercase -> lowercase); (e) input-language or translation-target switch; (f) preference reversal (prefer concise -> prefer verbose). Grid over n_pre in {0,2,4,8,16,32,64} x n_post in {1,2,4,8,16,32} with 200+ prompts per cell. Models: Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct (and base), Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B/14B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B, OLMo-2 (for pretraining-data transparency), plus GPT-4o-mini via API for a closed-model check.
2) Reference-learner comparison. Fit (i) an exchangeable Bayesian posterior over the finite rule set given all demos, (ii) a geometrically discounted likelihood learner with discount gamma, (iii) a last-k-only learner. Metric: which predicts model accuracy/logit ratios best (log-likelihood, R^2) and the implied gamma per model/scale. Primary quantitative test of the switch-cost law: regress post-switch accuracy on n_post/(n_pre+n_post) vs. on n_post alone; report 'adaptation half-life' h(n_pre) = number of post-switch demos to reach 50% of oracle (n_pre=0) accuracy, and test h ~ c * n_pre (linear) vs. constant.
3) Mechanistic analysis. Extract task vectors for rule A and rule B from clean stationary prompts (mean residual-stream activation at the final delimiter, per layer). For drifted prompts, regress the observed activation onto span{v_A, v_B} and test whether the fitted weight on v_B matches n_post/(n_pre+n_post). Identify task-encoding heads by (i) attention mass on demonstration label tokens, (ii) causal patching: replace head outputs with clean rule-B-prompt outputs and measure recovered post-switch accuracy. Also train a per-layer linear probe on the residual stream to classify 'a rule change has occurred in this context' and measure detection latency vs. behavioral adaptation latency (does the model 'know' before it acts?).
4) Interventions (all training-free, evaluated on held-out drift families). (a) Prompt-level: explicit instruction 'the rule changed; use only the most recent examples'; also re-stating recent demos. (b) Attention discounting: add log(gamma) * (number of demonstration blocks between query and key) to attention logits, applied only in the identified task-encoding heads; sweep gamma in [0.5,1.0]; ablate 'all heads' vs 'task heads' vs 'random heads'. (c) Probe-gated discounting: apply (b) only when the drift probe fires, so stationary prompts are unaffected. (d) KV-block eviction: drop pre-switch demonstration KV entries as an upper-bound oracle. Metrics: post-switch accuracy vs. oracle rule-B-only prompt, stationary-ICL regression (accuracy on 20 standard ICL tasks with no drift), false-positive rate of the probe, and compute overhead.
5) Small-model pretraining study (stability-plasticity). Train ~10M-parameter GPT-2-style transformers from scratch on synthetic ICL tasks (linear regression, sparse parity) with meta-training mixtures containing p in {0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0} fraction of drifting sequences (one or more mid-sequence task switches). Measure (i) post-switch adaptation half-life, (ii) stationary in-context sample efficiency, (iii) implied discount gamma, and (iv) whether induction-head-like circuits become recency-gated. This tests whether stale-evidence anchoring is a consequence of stationary pretraining data rather than an architectural limit.
6) Optional realism check: multi-turn instruction-revision dialogues (revised constraints after several compliant turns) scored with an LLM judge and rule-based checkers, testing whether the same switch-cost law appears in naturalistic settings.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Models may already be strongly recency-biased, so no anchoring appears; this is still a publishable negative result that overturns the exchangeable-Bayes picture, and the reference-learner fits quantify gamma either way. (2) Instruction-tuned models may over-rely on the most recent example, confounding drift adaptation with generic recency bias — controlled by including within-rule order permutations and matched no-drift controls. (3) Task vectors may not be linearly decomposable into span{v_A,v_B}; we report subspace-fit quality and fall back to logit-difference-based mixture estimates. (4) Attention discounting may hurt long-range copying and instruction following; mitigated by head selectivity, probe gating, and explicit stationary-regression evaluation. (5) Some drift families are semantically confusable with noisy labels; we include a noisy-label control (same number of 'wrong' labels but interleaved rather than blocked) to show blocked drift is qualitatively different. (6) Compute limits us to <=14B open models locally plus small API checks; scale trends may be incomplete.

Name: eliminative_icl_negative_evidence
Title: What LLMs Fail to Learn From What Isn't So: Eliminative In-Context Learning and the Copy-Head Bottleneck
Short Hypothesis: In-context learning is driven by positive label copying (induction/copy heads), so LLMs extract far less information from *negative* (eliminative) demonstrations than from information-equivalent positive ones — and in the limit they treat 'x is NOT y' as evidence *for* y. We test this with an exactly information-matched positive-vs-negative demonstration design (in binary tasks a negative demo is logically identical to a positive one), quantify the shortfall in bits relative to a Bayesian oracle, localize it to copy-suppression-deficient heads, and repair it training-free.
Related Work: Four literatures touch this but none isolate it. (1) Negation in LMs: Kassner & Schütze (2020), Ettinger (2020), Hosseini et al. (2021), and inverse-scaling on negated prompts (Jang et al. 2023) show LMs mishandle negation in *task instructions or single sentences*; we instead ask whether negation can serve as *learning signal inside demonstrations*, an evidence-integration question rather than a semantic-comprehension one. (2) Label-corruption ICL: Min et al. (2022) show random labels barely hurt; Wei et al. (2023) study flipped labels; Yoo et al. (2022) revisit ground-truth sensitivity. Crucially, in all of these the wrong labels are *unmarked* — the model is never told an example is a counterexample, so nothing tests eliminative inference. Our negative demos are explicitly marked and are information-equivalent to positive ones by construction. (3) Contrastive/negative-example prompting methods (c-ICL, contrastive CoT, 'learning from mistakes' prompts) *engineer* gains from positive+negative pairs but report only end-task accuracy; they never ask how many bits of the available eliminative information the model actually uses, nor why it fails, and they confound the negative signal with extra tokens/content. (4) Bayesian accounts of ICL (Xie et al. 2022; Bayesian scaling laws, Arora et al. 2024) and concept/task-vector mechanisms assume positive i.i.d. (x,y) evidence; a Bayesian learner handles negative evidence for free, so our design is a sharp falsification test of the Bayesian story that stationary positive-only prompts cannot provide. We additionally connect the deficit to a concrete circuit story (induction/copy heads and copy-suppression heads, Olsson et al. 2022; McDougall et al. 2023) and to a practical failure: agents that keep past wrong answers in context repeat them.
Abstract: Every study of in-context learning feeds the model positive evidence: examples of what the answer *is*. Human and Bayesian learners also learn from what the answer is *not*. We ask a simple question with a clean experimental handle: can LLMs learn in-context from explicitly negative demonstrations, and if not, why? Our key design is information matching. In a binary task, 'x is NOT negative' is logically identical to 'x is positive', so a negative demonstration carries exactly the same bits as a positive one; in a k-way task, a negative demonstration carries a precisely computable log(k/(k-1)) bits. This lets us define negative-evidence efficiency, the fraction of available eliminative information an LLM converts into accuracy, and to compare directly against a Bayesian oracle. Across open models (Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1, Gemma-2, OLMo-2, 0.5B-70B) and synthetic rule-induction, classification, and constraint-satisfaction tasks, we predict and test a strong asymmetry: negative demonstrations yield a small fraction of the gain of information-equivalent positive ones, and often *raise* the probability of the very label they exclude — negation-as-association. Mechanistically, we attribute this to label-copying induction heads that attend to the demonstration answer token while remaining largely insensitive to the polarity marker, showing via per-head logit attribution, polarity probes, and causal patching where polarity information exists but fails to be routed into suppression. We then repair the deficit training-free: (i) verbalized elimination that rewrites negative demos into positive ones, and (ii) polarity-gated inversion of copy-head contributions, recovering most of the oracle gap. Finally, small-transformer meta-training shows eliminative ICL emerges only when pretraining data contains negative evidence, and coincides with the birth of anti-induction heads. As an application, we show that keeping past wrong answers in an agent's context increases repetition of those exact errors, and that our fix reduces it.
Experiments:
1) Information-matched benchmark. Tasks: (a) binary classification (SST-2, AGNews restricted to 2 classes, RTE, BoolQ) where each demo is rendered either positively ('Input: x / Label: positive') or negatively ('Input: x / Label: NOT negative'), with the label set stated in the instruction so the two are logically equivalent; (b) k-way classification (TREC k=6, Banking77 subsets k=4/8/16, synthetic color/shape categories) with negative demos excluding one wrong label; (c) synthetic rule induction with an explicit finite hypothesis space (boolean concepts over 5 features, ~100 candidate rules) where positive and negative examples can be exactly information-matched by Bayesian bit count; (d) constraint tasks (generate a word satisfying constraints, with negative demos = rejected candidates). Grid over n_demos in {0,2,4,8,16,32}, 300 prompts per cell, 5 prompt formats and 3 negation phrasings ('NOT', 'is wrong', 'incorrect answer:') to separate wording from mechanism. Models: Qwen2.5-0.5/1.5/7/14B, Llama-3.1-8B & 70B (base and instruct), Gemma-2-9B, OLMo-2-7B, plus GPT-4o-mini/Claude-Haiku API checks.
2) Primary metrics. Negative-Evidence Efficiency NEE = (acc_neg - acc_0)/(acc_pos - acc_0) at matched information. Bits-extracted: fit accuracy as a function of Bayesian-oracle posterior entropy reduction for positive and negative streams; report the ratio of effective bits. Negation-as-association test: sign and magnitude of Δlogit for the *excluded* label relative to the no-demo baseline (per-model, bootstrap CIs). Also report mixed prompts (m positive + n negative) to test additivity.
3) Bayesian-oracle comparison. Exact posterior over the finite hypothesis space for tasks (a) and (c); plot model accuracy vs oracle accuracy as a function of demo count, separately for positive-only, negative-only, and mixed streams. This yields the headline figure: positive ICL tracks the oracle; negative ICL saturates far below it.
4) Mechanistic analysis (on 7-9B models with hooks). (i) Per-head direct logit attribution to the excluded label token; identify heads whose output writes *toward* the negated label. (ii) Attention pattern analysis: does head attention to the demo answer token change when the polarity marker flips? Quantify a polarity-sensitivity score per head. (iii) Linear probes at each layer on the residual stream at the delimiter for 'the last demo was negative' — measure whether polarity is linearly decodable (information present) despite behavioral insensitivity (routing failure). (iv) Causal patching: patch polarity-probe direction or specific head outputs from a matched positive prompt and measure behavioral change; also ablate copy-suppression heads (McDougall-style) to test whether they are the missing machinery.
5) Training-free interventions, evaluated on held-out tasks. (a) Verbalized elimination: an instruction plus one worked example telling the model to first rewrite each negative demo as the implied positive statement (and a CoT variant). (b) Hypothesis-space masking: constrained decoding that zeroes labels explicitly excluded by negative demos (upper bound / sanity oracle). (c) Polarity-gated copy inversion: for tokens inside negative demos, negate the contribution of the top-K identified copy heads to the label logits (implemented as a hook that subtracts the head's OV write on demo answer tokens), gated by the polarity probe; sweep K and gate threshold. Metrics: recovered fraction of oracle gap, degradation on 20 standard positive-only ICL tasks (must be ~0), and compute overhead.
6) Small-model meta-training study. Train ~10-20M parameter transformers from scratch on synthetic ICL rule-induction sequences with fraction p in {0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0} of negative-labeled examples. Measure (i) whether eliminative ICL emerges and at what p, (ii) sample efficiency of positive vs negative evidence, (iii) whether anti-induction / suppression heads appear (head-level copying score over training), (iv) transfer: does training with negative evidence on one rule family generalize to unseen families? This tests data-distribution vs architecture explanations.
7) Agentic application. Multi-turn setting on GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, and a simple tool-calling environment where the context contains the model's k previous *wrong* answers labeled as wrong. Metric: exact-repetition rate of a previously-listed wrong answer vs. a no-history control matched for token count (filled with irrelevant text), and accuracy. Then apply intervention (5a/5c) and re-measure. This links the mechanistic deficit to the widely reported failure of self-correction loops.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Strong instruction-tuned models may already handle explicit negation well on easy binary tasks, compressing NEE toward 1; we mitigate by including k-way and multi-negative-demo regimes where eliminative inference must be composed, and by reporting scale trends (the interesting result may be that NEE grows with scale but stays sub-Bayesian). (2) Negation phrasing is a confound; addressed with three phrasings, a symbol-only marker (e.g., 'x → y [✗]'), and format randomization. (3) Information matching is exact only when the label set is closed and stated; for open-ended constraint tasks we report qualitative rather than bit-level comparisons. (4) Copy-head attribution may be diffuse in larger models, weakening the mechanistic claim; we pre-register the probe/patching analysis as the primary mechanistic evidence with head attribution as support, and run mechanistic work on ≤9B models. (5) Interventions on attention writes may destabilize generation; we restrict them to demo answer-token positions and verify perplexity on held-out text. (6) Compute limits local hook-based work to ≤14B models; 70B and API models are behavioral-only.

Name: sampling_assumption_icl
Title: Suspicious Coincidences Are Not Suspicious to LLMs: Testing the Sampling Assumption Behind In-Context Learning
Short Hypothesis: Bayesian accounts of ICL specify a posterior over latent tasks but never test the *likelihood* that generates demonstrations. We hypothesize that LLMs implicitly assume demonstrations are weakly sampled (randomly observed) rather than strongly/pedagogically sampled (deliberately chosen from within the target concept), so they do not obey the size principle: their generalization breadth barely narrows as more mutually-consistent examples arrive, whereas humans and strong-sampling Bayes narrow exponentially. We can measure this as a single interpretable exponent alpha in p(x|h) ~ 1/|h|^alpha estimated from model behavior, show alpha ~ 0 for LLMs, show alpha is largely insensitive to explicit statements about how examples were chosen, and show alpha ~ 1 emerges in small transformers only when meta-training data are actually strongly sampled.
Related Work: (1) Bayesian views of ICL: Xie et al. (2022) implicit Bayesian inference; Bayesian scaling laws for ICL (Arora et al., 2024); Bayes' Power for Explaining ICL Generalizations (2025); task recognition vs. task learning (Pan et al., 2023; Lin & Lee, 2024). All of these assume a likelihood form and fit accuracy/posterior-concentration curves; none identifies *which sampling assumption* the model's implicit likelihood encodes, even though this is the single degree of freedom that determines whether more consistent examples sharpen a hypothesis at all. (2) Cognitive science: Tenenbaum & Griffiths' number game and the size principle, Xu & Tenenbaum's word learning, and pedagogical/teaching-by-example models (Shafto, Goodman & Griffiths). Recent cognitive-science probes have run GPT-style models on number-game-like items, but they report accuracy or qualitative similarity to humans on fixed example sets; they do not (a) estimate the sampling exponent, (b) causally manipulate the sampling frame while holding the examples fixed, or (c) connect the result to pretraining data statistics or to practical ICL. (3) ICL demonstration selection (similarity retrieval, ambiguity-aware selection, ConDS) implicitly *is* pedagogical sampling: a retriever hand-picks examples. Our results imply a mismatch between how demonstrations are produced (curated) and how models interpret them (as random observations), which no prior work articulates or tests. (4) Mechanistic ICL work (concept encoding-decoding, contextualize-then-aggregate, task vectors) explains how task information is aggregated but not what statistical assumption governs aggregation. Our contribution is a falsifiable, one-parameter characterization of ICL's implicit likelihood, a within-item causal test using sampling-frame metadata, a data-distributional explanation via small-transformer meta-training, and a training-free repair.
Abstract: Given the examples {16, 8, 2, 64}, humans confidently infer 'powers of two' rather than 'even numbers', because a random sample of even numbers would be a suspicious coincidence. This inference requires a specific likelihood - the size principle, p(x|h) proportional to 1/|h| - which follows from assuming examples were drawn from *within* the concept (strong or pedagogical sampling). Every Bayesian account of in-context learning posits a posterior over latent tasks, yet none has asked which sampling assumption LLMs encode. We answer this with a simple, quantitative probe: we present LLMs with nested-hypothesis concept-learning prompts (numbers, taxonomic categories, regexes/string patterns, and label-scope classification) in which the examples are consistent with both a narrow and a broad hypothesis, vary the number of consistent examples n from 1 to 8, and measure the generalization gradient over probe items that discriminate the hypotheses. Fitting a one-parameter Bayesian family with likelihood 1/|h|^alpha to model behavior yields an interpretable 'sampling exponent'. Our central prediction is that LLMs sit near alpha = 0 (weak sampling): breadth is driven by surface similarity to the examples, not by the improbability of the coincidence, so redundant consistent examples buy almost no narrowing - unlike humans, who track alpha near 1. We further test whether alpha is a controllable knob by stating the sampling frame explicitly ('a teacher chose these to be maximally informative' vs 'these were randomly encountered'), which changes the normative answer while holding examples fixed. We then explain the deficit: small transformers meta-trained on positive-only strongly-sampled concepts do acquire alpha near 1, whereas incidental/weakly-sampled meta-training yields alpha near 0, indicating a data-distributional rather than architectural origin. Finally, we show a cheap repair (hypothesis-enumeration-with-size CoT) that recovers most human-like narrowing and reduces overgeneralization in a practical rule-induction task, and we show that similarity-based demonstration retrieval systematically produces prompts whose pedagogical information LLMs cannot exploit.
Experiments:
1) Benchmark of nested-hypothesis concept learning (4 domains, all with explicitly enumerable hypothesis spaces so exact Bayesian references can be computed). (a) Number game: domain 1-100, hypothesis space of ~60 mathematical (multiples, powers, primes, ranges) and interval hypotheses, matching Tenenbaum's setup so published human generalization data can be used as a baseline. (b) Taxonomic categories: examples like {dalmatian} vs {dalmatian, poodle, beagle, corgi}; probes at subordinate/basic/superordinate levels (WordNet-derived, with hypothesis sizes estimated from WordNet extension counts). (c) String/regex induction: strings consistent with both a narrow pattern (e.g., 'a^n b^n') and a broad one ('contains a and b'); hypothesis sizes computed exactly over bounded-length strings. (d) Label-scope classification: an ICL prompt gives k positive examples of a category label (all drawn from a narrow subcategory) and we measure whether the model applies the label to superordinate items - the practical face of overgeneralization.
2) Core manipulation and metric. For each item, vary n in {1,2,3,4,6,8} where all examples are consistent with both narrow and broad hypotheses and (critically) are *maximally uninformative individually* (no example excludes the broad hypothesis). Elicit generalization probabilities for held-out probe items via next-token yes/no logits (and a verbalized-probability variant). Primary quantity: narrowing slope = d/dn of P(probe in concept) for broad-only probes. Fit the one-parameter Bayesian family with likelihood proportional to 1/|h|^alpha and prior fixed from the enumerated hypothesis space; report maximum-likelihood alpha_hat with bootstrap CIs per model, per domain. Secondary: KL divergence of model generalization gradients from alpha=0 and alpha=1 Bayes; correlation with human data for the number game. Also run a 'redundancy control': repeating the *same* example n times (which should not narrow under any account) to verify the measured narrowing is not a token-frequency artifact.
3) Sampling-frame causal test. Hold examples fixed and vary a one-sentence frame: (i) 'A teacher chose these examples to help you identify the rule as precisely as possible' (strong/pedagogical), (ii) 'These examples were encountered at random while browsing' (weak), (iii) 'A teacher chose these examples but is only allowed to show positive examples' (strong), (iv) no frame. A normative learner shifts alpha between 0 and 1; measure delta alpha_hat per frame. Also test a 'teacher stopped here' cue ('the teacher showed only these') vs 'more examples exist'.
4) Scale and model family sweep. Qwen2.5 0.5/1.5/7/14B, Llama-3.1-8B/70B (base and instruct), Gemma-2-2B/9B, OLMo-2-7B, plus GPT-4o-mini and Claude-Haiku via API. Questions: does alpha_hat grow with scale? Does instruction tuning or RLHF change it? Does reasoning-style prompting (CoT) or a reasoning model (e.g., a distilled R1) change it? Base-vs-instruct comparison separates pretraining statistics from alignment.
5) Small-transformer meta-training study (origin of alpha). Train ~10-20M parameter decoder-only transformers on synthetic in-context concept learning over a known hypothesis space (nested intervals / divisibility rules over a discrete domain) under three data-generating processes: (i) strong sampling (examples drawn i.i.d. uniformly from the true concept's extension), (ii) weak sampling (x drawn uniformly from the domain, then labeled +/-, with only positives shown), (iii) mixtures with fraction p strong. Estimate alpha_hat of the trained model on held-out concepts. Prediction: (i) yields alpha near 1, (ii) yields alpha near 0, and alpha_hat increases monotonically with p. Additional condition: append an explicit sampling-frame token to sequences to test whether a model can learn to *condition* alpha on metadata - the trainable analogue of Experiment 3, telling us whether the LLM failure is 'cannot represent' or 'never had to'.
6) Training-free repairs, evaluated on held-out domains. (a) Hypothesis-enumeration CoT: instruct the model to list candidate rules, estimate each rule's extension size, and prefer smaller extensions when all rules fit; (b) size-scored reranking: sample candidate rules from the model, compute/ask for extension sizes, score by n*log(1/|h|) + log prior, and answer with the argmax (a scaffolded Bayesian learner); (c) self-generated probes: model proposes discriminating test items and answers as if it observed the teacher's silence. Metrics: recovered alpha_hat, human-correlation on number game, false-positive rate on superordinate probes in the label-scope task, and cost in tokens. Control that repairs do not hurt standard ICL classification accuracy on 15 conventional tasks.
7) Practical consequence for demonstration selection. Using standard similarity retrievers (SBERT/BM25) on classification datasets, measure how often the retrieved k-shot set is consistent with a narrow-but-wrong hypothesis (e.g., all retrieved positives share a spurious surface feature), and show that LLMs fail to narrow when narrowing is correct and fail to broaden when the retrieved set is unrepresentative. Compare 'diversity-sampled' vs 'similarity-retrieved' demonstrations under our alpha framework to give a principled reinterpretation of known selection heuristics.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Strong models may already display size-principle-like narrowing on the number game because that dataset and Tenenbaum's analysis are in pretraining data; mitigated by the novel regex/string, taxonomic, and label-scope domains with randomized surface forms, and by a contamination check (asking models to recall the paradigm). (2) alpha_hat is only identifiable given a hypothesis space and prior; we fix these to the standard enumerations, report sensitivity to prior choice, and additionally report model-free narrowing slopes that require no fitted prior. (3) Eliciting calibrated generalization probabilities from LLMs is noisy; addressed via logit-based yes/no with format randomization, order-balanced probes, verbalized-probability and forced-choice replications, and multiple paraphrases. (4) A null result on the sampling-frame manipulation is possible but informative (it shows the sampling assumption is not a controllable knob, motivating training-side fixes and connecting to Experiment 5). (5) Small-transformer results may not transfer to LLM scale; we present them as a mechanistic existence proof about data distributions, not a claim about LLM training. (6) Extension sizes for natural-language categories are only approximate; we use WordNet counts plus human-annotated size rankings and report rank-based analyses robust to size mis-estimation.

Name: stochastic_icl_noise_blindness
Title: Can In-Context Learners Learn a Distribution? Aleatoric Noise Blindness in ICL and an Activation-Level Cure
Short Hypothesis: Every ICL benchmark assumes a deterministic latent function from x to y, so we do not know whether LLMs can infer a *stochastic* rule in context. We hypothesize an asymmetry we call noise blindness: when demonstrations are generated by a known noisy rule (P(y=A|x)=p), LLMs' predictive distributions transmit only a small fraction of the in-context aleatoric rate (log-odds slope beta << 1, i.e. mode collapse toward the majority label), while simultaneously being nearly insensitive to the epistemic uncertainty that should shrink with the number of demonstrations. Because the noise rate is nonetheless linearly decodable from the residual stream, this is a routing failure that a single training-free steering/recalibration knob can largely repair.
Related Work: (1) Bayesian accounts of ICL (Xie et al. 2022; Bayesian scaling laws, Arora et al. 2024; Bayes' Power for Explaining ICL Generalizations, 2025) and PFN/TabPFN work show trained-for-purpose in-context learners approximate posterior predictives, but LLM-side evaluations score *accuracy* or posterior concentration over tasks, never asking whether the model reproduces a *known* conditional label distribution; a Bayesian learner gets aleatoric noise for free, so this is a sharp, previously untested prediction. (2) Noisy-label ICL: Min et al. (2022) randomize labels (maximal noise) and Wei et al. (2023) flip labels, but both report accuracy only; robustness work such as ConDS (2025) treats noise as a nuisance to *filter out* rather than a quantity to *estimate*. (3) LLM calibration (contextual calibration, Zhao et al. 2021; ECE studies) measures confidence vs. correctness, where the ground-truth uncertainty is unknown and confounded with model competence; our synthetic design supplies the exact target distribution, letting us cleanly factor predictive uncertainty into an aleatoric transmission coefficient and an epistemic n-sensitivity term. (4) Distributional-alignment work (ChaosNLI/soft-label prediction, benchmarks of LLM opinion distributions) asks whether models match human label distributions *zero-shot from priors*; we instead ask whether the distribution can be *taught in context*, which is the ICL question and yields a different diagnosis and fix. (5) Mechanistic ICL work (induction heads; task/function vectors; concept encoding-decoding) explains how a single deterministic task label is extracted; nothing there predicts or represents a scalar noise level. We contribute: a stochastic-rule ICL benchmark with exact ground truth, a two-number characterization (beta, epsilon) of ICL uncertainty, evidence that noise rate is encoded-but-unused, a homoscedastic-vs-heteroscedastic dissociation, and a cheap activation-level repair validated on real annotator-disagreement data.
Abstract: In-context learning is universally evaluated on deterministic tasks: there is one correct label per input. But most real prediction problems are stochastic, and a competent learner should infer not just the mapping but its noise level. We ask whether LLMs can learn a distribution in context. We build prompts whose demonstrations are drawn from an explicitly noisy rule, P(y=A|x)=p with p known to the experimenter, and compare the model's next-token distribution over label verbalizers with the exact Bayesian posterior predictive. This design yields two interpretable numbers per model: an aleatoric transmission coefficient beta, the slope of model log-odds on true in-context log-odds, and an epistemic sensitivity epsilon, how much predictive entropy shrinks as demonstrations accumulate under a deterministic rule. We predict and test noise blindness: beta far below 1 (predictive distributions collapse toward the majority label, ignoring in-context stochasticity) together with small epsilon (confidence barely tracks evidence quantity), so LLMs' predictive uncertainty is largely decoupled from both components of the ground truth. We further dissociate homoscedastic from heteroscedastic (input-dependent) noise, showing the latter is essentially unlearned. Mechanistically, we train linear probes showing the in-context noise rate *is* linearly decodable from mid-layer activations, i.e. the information is present but not routed to the output; steering along this decoded direction, or an affine logit recalibration conditioned on the decoded rate, recovers most of the gap to the Bayesian oracle at negligible cost. Small transformers meta-trained on stochastic tasks achieve beta near 1, showing the deficit is distributional, not architectural. Finally, on ChaosNLI and other multi-annotator datasets our repair improves prediction of human label distributions over standard few-shot prompting.
Experiments:
1) Stochastic ICL benchmark (exact ground truth). Families: (a) Bernoulli label noise on classification: a real task (SST-2, AG News, RTE, TREC) whose demonstration labels are resampled so that the true rule holds with probability p in {0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9,1.0}; (b) pure abstract rules with no semantic prior (tokens 'foo'/'bar' assigned to symbolic inputs with rate p), which removes the model's pretraining prior as a confound; (c) coin/urn tasks (context lists outcomes of a biased process; query asks for the next outcome); (d) in-context regression with known observation noise (y = w x + noise, sigma varied), scored by whether sampled/verbalized predictions match the correct predictive spread; (e) heteroscedastic variant, where p depends on an observable feature of x (e.g., p=0.9 for inputs of type 1 and p=0.6 for type 2, or p varying with a stated attribute). Grid: n_demos in {2,4,8,16,32,64,128}, 300 prompts per cell, 4 prompt formats, label-word and order randomization. Models: Qwen2.5 0.5/1.5/7/14B, Llama-3.1-8B and 70B (base and instruct), Gemma-2-2B/9B, OLMo-2-7B, plus GPT-4o-mini / Claude-Haiku behavioral checks (logprobs where available, else repeated sampling to estimate the distribution).
2) Primary metrics. (i) Aleatoric transmission coefficient beta: regress model log-odds of the majority label on the exact posterior-predictive log-odds (Beta-Bernoulli with uniform prior over the empirical context) across all (p, n) cells; report beta with bootstrap CIs, plus intercept (bias) and R^2. Predict beta << 1. (ii) Epistemic sensitivity epsilon: for p=1.0, slope of model log-odds vs. log n, compared with the Bayesian slope. (iii) Distributional error: KL(oracle || model) and ECE-against-oracle. (iv) Sampling test: does temperature-1 sampling recover the frequency p (probability matching) or collapse (maximizing)? (v) Marginal-vs-conditional control: prompts where the label marginal is 0.5 but conditional rates differ by input type, to verify the model is not merely copying the global base rate. (vi) Heteroscedastic score: per-group beta in family (e).
3) Behavioral controls and simple prompting baselines. Does an explicit statement of the noise ('labels are noisy about 30% of the time') fix it? Does an instruction to output a probability, or a verbalized-counting CoT ('count how many demonstrations of each label, then give the fraction'), fix it? Does many-shot (128 demos) help or hurt? Does instruction tuning change beta (base vs. instruct)? These separate 'cannot represent' from 'does not by default'.
4) Mechanistic analysis (7-9B models with hooks). Train ridge/logistic probes at every layer on the residual stream at the final delimiter to predict the in-context noise rate p (and, in the heteroscedastic case, the group-specific rate), using held-out p values and held-out tasks; report R^2 by layer as evidence for encoded-but-unused noise information. Causal tests: (i) patch the probe direction from a high-noise prompt into a low-noise prompt and measure the change in output entropy; (ii) per-head direct logit attribution to the minority label to find whether copy/induction heads dominate and drive collapse; (iii) ablate top copy heads and re-measure beta.
5) Training-free repairs, evaluated on held-out task families. (a) Activation steering: add alpha * (decoded noise direction) to the residual stream, with alpha calibrated once on a synthetic development set; (b) probe-conditioned affine logit recalibration: rescale label logits by a temperature that is an affine function of the probe's decoded noise rate; (c) scaffolded counting oracle (upper bound). Metrics: recovered beta and KL to oracle, plus a strict no-regression check on 15 standard clean ICL tasks (accuracy must be unchanged) and negligible latency overhead.
6) Small-transformer meta-training control. Train ~10-20M-parameter decoder-only transformers on synthetic ICL sequences whose tasks are (i) deterministic only, (ii) stochastic with p sampled per sequence, (iii) mixtures with fraction q stochastic. Measure beta, epsilon, and heteroscedastic learning as a function of q. Prediction: beta near 1 emerges only with stochastic meta-training, establishing a data-distributional origin, and providing a reference for what a well-calibrated in-context learner looks like at small scale.
7) Real-data validation: predicting human label distributions. On ChaosNLI (100 annotations/item), MD-Agreement, and a toxicity dataset with per-annotator labels, build few-shot prompts whose demonstrations include *disagreeing* labels for the same item (or repeated items with different labels) and evaluate the model's predicted label distribution against human distributions (KL, total variation, correlation of entropy). Compare (i) majority-label prompting, (ii) disagreement-revealing prompting, (iii) our probe-conditioned recalibration, and (iv) verbalized-counting CoT. This shows the synthetic deficit predicts a practically important failure and that the fix transfers.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Large instruct models may already probability-match on simple coin tasks, compressing beta toward 1; the abstract-token, heteroscedastic, and low-n regimes are designed to remain discriminative, and a scale trend (beta rising but sub-oracle) is itself a publishable characterization. (2) Label-verbalizer logits are sensitive to format and surface bias; mitigated by format/label randomization, contextual-calibration baselines, and reporting logit-difference-based measures. (3) With small n, the model cannot distinguish sampling noise from a shifted rule, so oracle comparisons must use the exact posterior predictive (which we compute) rather than the true p; we report both. (4) Probes may pick up correlates (e.g., label imbalance) rather than a noise-rate code; addressed with held-out p values, balanced-marginal controls, and causal patching. (5) Steering may distort generation quality; restricted to the query position and verified with held-out perplexity and clean-ICL no-regression tests. (6) Human-disagreement datasets conflate annotator noise with genuine ambiguity, so real-data results are corroborative rather than definitive. (7) Local mechanistic work is limited to <=14B models; 70B and API models are behavioral only.
